SCENE
A wide 16:9 landscape illustration, edge to edge, filling the whole frame.
a mixed forest of birch and maple at the peak of autumn colour, a leaf-covered path winding through it, a small wooden footbridge over a stream, low afternoon sun through the canopy

CAMERA
Camera: at a standing adult's eye level, looking straight into the scene from the middle distance. The horizon sits across the upper third.

THE THREE CHILDREN
Three particular children are the subject of this picture:
  1. The eldest (portrait 1): a girl of 8 with black hair cut in a chin-length bob with a straight fringe. Tall and lanky, the tallest by a clear margin.
  2. The middle one (portrait 2): a girl of 6 with red curly hair to the shoulders, usually tied back in one puffy ponytail. Small-framed and quick, with a scatter of freckles across her nose.
  3. The youngest (portrait 3): a boy of 4 with short dark-brown hair, cropped close at the sides and a little spiky on top. Stocky and solid, with a round face and short legs.
Their ages show in their size and the difference is plain at a glance. Child 1 is the tallest. Child 2 is shorter: the top of her head comes up to child 1's chin. Child 3 is much the smallest: the top of his head comes up to child 1's chest, and to child 2's chin. Keep that order however they are posed — standing, sitting, crouching or mid-air.
Hair is how they are recognised, so each child's hair colour and hairstyle are clear and uncovered — no hat, hood or helmet hides it. In cold weather use earmuffs, a headband, a scarf, or a hat pushed back with the hair plainly showing.
Everything else about them is yours to invent, fresh for this picture: their clothes (ordinary everyday clothes for this weather and season, in colours that suit the picture, each child dressed differently from the others), their expressions, and their poses.
HOW FAR AWAY EACH ONE IS. They are not all at the same distance, and this is the picture's game — one of them is meant to take a moment to find.
  Child 1 is in the middle distance, partly behind or among other things.
  Child 2 is in the middle distance, partly behind or among other things.
  Child 3 is near the front and easy to pick out at a glance.
Whatever their distance, the HEIGHT ORDER above still reads: child 1 is the tallest child and child 3 the smallest, so a nearer young child is never drawn taller on the page than an older one further back.
The three attached pictures are their portraits, in the order listed. The portraits say WHO each child is, not how to draw them: render the children with exactly the same technique as everything else in this picture.
They are the three nearest and largest children in the picture. Any other children in the crowd are far off and clearly smaller.

WHAT THEY ARE DOING
The three of them together: all three building a den out of long sticks together.

LAYOUT
All three are in the front half of the picture, between the foreground and the middle distance, and each is at least a quarter of the picture's height tall — large enough that hair and face read clearly from across a room. Each child's face is towards the viewer (front on, three-quarter or profile) with head and body turned the same way.
Spread them across the scene with clear ground between them: at least a tenth of the picture's width from one child to the next, even when they share one activity. Not a huddle, and not a row along the bottom edge.

EVERYONE ELSE
Behind and around them the place is busy and full of life: a fox, a deer at the treeline, squirrels with acorns, mushrooms on a fallen log, birds, a woodpile, hikers with backpacks, a family on a rug.
Every person in the picture is fully clothed, in a top and bottoms, whatever the season or the activity.
Hidden somewhere in the picture is a medium-sized black-and-white border collie with a long coat and pricked ears. He is a REAL dog of a known size, and he is the thing everything else in the picture is scaled against: standing on all fours his shoulders come up to child 3's hip, and nose to tail he is almost exactly as long as child 3 is tall. Every other object in the picture — a tree, a chair, a piece of fruit — is the size it would really be beside a dog that size. He is hiding — peering out of long grass, half behind a tree trunk, a rock, a bush or a fence — never in the centre, never the biggest thing in the scene, and never posed with the children.

STYLE
Style: children's colouring-book cartoon. VERY THICK uniform black outlines on every shape, flat solid fills, no shading, no gradients, no texture.
Colours: flat solid fills from this palette — sand #E7DCC9, deep sand #E0D3BC, tan #B9A888, brown #7D6B57, cream #FFFDF9, blue #0D3399, magenta #D02076, amber #FFAE14, green #128239, red #A8221B, and near-black #171310 for the outlines only. The sky is plain flat sand #E7DCC9. Every shape is BRIGHTLY and FLATLY coloured.

RULES
The top of the picture, right across its width, is the quietest part of it: open sky or a plain ceiling in one smooth wash of colour, with at most a bird, a star or a distant hill in it, and nothing else drawn up there.
There is no writing anywhere in the picture: no letters, numbers, words, watermarks or frames, and nothing in it carries lettering.
